description: We are given the new frame of astrophysics!
summary:
With SwitchTensor, anyone can search for moving or changing objects using real NASA SPHEREx images in a web browser. No account, installation or coding is required.
It's simple by design.  It gathers every SPHEREx image of a given patch of sky and displays them in time order: anything that moves or changes will stand out. Clicking on an object shows its spectrum in SPHEREx's 102 colours. Multiple data sources add known objects and extend the baseline back to 2010.
 Lite mode is the default setting and only includes what a beginner needs, while Pro mode adds measurement tools.
It's fast because we've reduced the whole sky. A field built from the full SPHEREx images would require downloading hundreds of MB. We have processed the entire SPHEREx archive into a compact, pre-cut copy of the sky, with one exposure per sky cell, detector and visit. Now, a field loads a few MB instead of hundreds, straight from public storage, and the site needs no server of its own. Full depth from NASA's original images on AWS is just a click away.
details:
Normally, finding a moving object in SPHEREx data means querying the archive, downloading hundreds of megabytes and writing a pipeline. SwitchTensor only needs one thing from you – type a name or coordinates, and it'll blink the SPHEREx visits of that sky in time order. What jumps is moving; what flickers is changing.

We use external astronomical data (e.g. Gaia and WISE) in three one-click checks: checking the object's spectrum and colour, overlaying rings to identify known stars, and viewing longer-baseline imagery. The advanced features are still available. We provide six built-in practice targets with hints and answers to help new users learn the workflow.

How it works

A field from the full SPHEREx images means downloading hundreds of megabytes, and most of these are the same sky seen again within days. We made the whole archive into one 8-bit cut-out per 2° sky cell, detector and visit (all cells, on Hugging Face). This process of quantisation makes only a small difference to how humans see things. However, a field now loads a few megabytes, which is two orders of magnitude less. The "Load full depth" option still uses NASA's original images from AWS and displays them in the browser. We don't use a server: we have static files on Cloudflare, data on AWS and Hugging Face.

Benifits

No account, no install, no code, and a few MB per Field, so it works in any browser on a home or school connection.

Creativity

  • Instead of checking the archive for every visitor, we did the hard work just once for the whole sky.
  • SwitchTensor provides Lite mode and Pro mode. Lite mode contains only beginner needed features, and expert features stay in Pro mode.
  • A colour view compares each star with the Field's own ordinary stars, so a red, cold object stands out without any calibration.
  • The whole view is in the URL, so you can share a find by sending a link.
  • A community reports service is being set up. This will let anyone submit a candidate, see what others reported nearby, and thank them.

Intended impact

SwitchTensor helps students, schoolers and citizen scientists get started by letting them look through SPHEREx's growing all-sky archive, even though they don't have their own pipeline.

Factors we considered

  • SPHEREx has only 2 or 3 Epochs per Field so far, so we added WISE for a baseline of years.
  • The reduced sky is for looking, not photometry; full data is one click away.
  • What did not serve a first-time user moved to Pro Mode.

Tools and languages

TypeScript, WebGL2 and Vite (web app); Python, Astropy and NumPy (sky reduction); Cloudflare, AWS Open Data and Hugging Face (hosting and data). Code licence: Apache 2.0.
